Yield
YEELD
v.
From Old English gieldan, “to pay, render, give back.” Renders the Greek paristēmi, “to present, place beside, yield” (the technical Romans 6 verb), and the Hebrew nāthan, “to give,” and ‘āsah, “to make, produce.”

Biblical Definition

To yield, in the central New Testament sense, is to present—deliberately, willingly, irrevocably—the members of one’s body to a master, for use as instruments. Paul’s great Romans 6 charter is unmistakable: neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin: but yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God. The picture is of a regenerate man, raised with Christ, choosing day by day to whom he will present his body, his tongue, his eyes, his hands, his thought-life, his time, his money, his sexuality, his strength: to sin as a deposed master, or to God as the new and rightful Lord. Yielding in this sense is not passive surrender but active presentation; it is not a one-time crisis decision but the daily disposition of the believer in real moral choices; and it is the precise hinge on which practical sanctification turns. The man who yields his members to sin will be the servant of sin to whom he yields; the man who yields his members to God will, in the very act, be acting out the new identity that grace has already conferred. Yielding has a second sense in Scripture: the bearing of fruit (the ground yields her increase; the field yields a harvest; the saint, abiding in the Vine, yields fruit unto God). The two senses converge: the man who yields his members to God yields, by that very yielding, the fruit of righteousness in his life. A third sense in James 3 commends the wisdom from above as willing to yield—eupeithēs, easy to be entreated, open, persuadable, not stiff-necked in self-will. All three senses are biblical, and all three describe the Christian: a man who has presented his members to God, who bears the fruit of righteousness in his life, and whose temper is open and reasonable, not rigid and contentious.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines YIELD as to give in return for labor expended; to produce, as fruit, profit, issues; to give up, to resign, to surrender; in scripture, to present or surrender to God.

expand to see more

YIELD, v.t. — 1. To produce, as fruit, profit, or issues; as, the earth yields her increase; the field yields a harvest. 2. To give in return for labor expended; to produce as a reward or recompence. 3. To give up, as claim or possession; to resign; to surrender; to relinquish. 4. To allow; to grant; to admit; as, to yield a point; to yield priority.

YIELD, v.i. — 1. To give up the contest; to submit. 2. To comply with; as, to yield to entreaty. 3. In scripture, to present or surrender oneself or one’s members to God (Rom 6:13).

Key Scripture

Romans 6:13 — "Neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin: but yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God."

Romans 6:19 — "...for as ye have yielded your members servants to uncleanness and to iniquity unto iniquity; even so now yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness."

James 3:17 — "But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy."

John 15:5 — "I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing."

Modern Corruption

Yielding is corrupted, on one side, by the passive-surrender misreading that empties the active presentation Paul commands; and on the other, by the cultural register that treats yielding as weakness—the rigid self-will that mistakes inflexibility for conviction and cannot bend even where the wisdom from above is plainly easy to be entreated.

expand to see more

Romans 6’s yielding is sometimes preached as if it were a single mystical surrender, a let-go-and-let-God passivity by which the believer turns the wheel over to God and ceases to act. The text says the opposite. Paul commands an active, deliberate presentation of the members of the body, day by day, in the real moral choices that fill a Christian life: yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness. The yielding is not passivity; it is precisely the act of presenting. The sanctified man is not the man who has stopped acting and waits for God to act through him; he is the man who, having been raised with Christ, deliberately presents his body, his tongue, his eyes, his time, his money, his sexuality, to God for use as instruments of righteousness—and who refuses to present them as instruments of unrighteousness. Recover the Romans 6 grammar and the doctrine returns to its New Testament force.

Yielding is also corrupted by the cultural register that treats it as weakness. The hard, contentious, stiff-necked temper that mistakes inflexibility for conviction is at home in much of the contemporary church, and the wisdom from above’s commendation of being easy to be entreated—a posture of being open, persuadable, willing to yield where Scripture and good cause counsel it—sounds to such ears like compromise. It is not. The biblical Christian yields his members to God in active presentation; he yields the fruit of righteousness in his life by abiding in the Vine; and he yields, in personal dealings, with the open and reasonable spirit James commends. The man who cannot yield in any of these three senses has not yet learned what the Spirit of God produces in His people—and is in no position to lead, teach, or contend for anything, because he cannot bend without breaking.

Hebrew Roots

Greek paristēmi (to present, place beside—the technical Rom 6 verb of yielding the body’s members to a master); Hebrew nāthan (to give) and ‘āsah (to produce, bear fruit); Greek eupeithēs (easy to be entreated, willing to yield—James 3:17).

expand to see more

Greek paristēmi (G3936) — to present, place beside, yield; the verb of Rom 6:13 and 12:1 (present your bodies a living sacrifice).

Greek eupeithēs (G2138) — easy to be entreated, willing to yield (James 3:17).

Hebrew nāthan (H5414) — to give; the base verb of giving and yielding in the OT.

Hebrew ‘āsah (H6213) — to do, make, produce; used of trees and ground yielding fruit (Gen 1:11-12).

Usage

"Yielding the members in Romans 6 is active presentation, not passive surrender—the daily choice of which master will use one’s body, tongue, eyes, and time."

"The branch in the Vine yields fruit; the wisdom from above yields to good cause; the saint yields his members to God—three biblical yieldings, one Christian."

"Stiff-necked inflexibility that mistakes itself for conviction has unlearned the easy-to-be-entreated temper of the heavenly wisdom; biblical yielding is strength, not weakness."
